articles.title: Low-Dose Glucocorticoids Adjunctive to Flow Diverter Therapy for Unruptured Intracranial Aneurysms Improve Cerebrovascular Outcomes
articles.titleEn: Low-Dose Glucocorticoids Adjunctive to Flow Diverter Therapy for Unruptured Intracranial Aneurysms Improve Cerebrovascular Outcomes
articles.abstract: Flow diverter (FD) implantation is standard for unruptured intracranial aneurysms (UIAs), but cerebrovascular complications persist. This nested study within a prospective multicenter cohort evaluates whether short-term, low-dose glucocorticoid use is associated with cerebrovascular outcomes after FD implantation. Propensity-score matching with exact matching on UIA location yielded 1327 patients (360 glucocorticoid-treated; 967 controls). Intravenous glucocorticoids, initiated within 2 hours of the FD procedure and administered for ≥2 days, were associated with fewer in-hospital cerebrovascular events (6.9% vs. 13.1%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.53) and major cerebrovascular events (4.7% vs. 12.4%; aOR, 0.37). Over a median 2-year follow-up, glucocorticoid use was also associated with fewer new-onset major cerebrovascular events (3.6% vs. 8.7%; adjusted hazard ratio, 0.41) and less in-stent stenosis (7.9% vs. 13.2%; aOR, 0.55). Findings remained robust in unmatched patients on sensitivity analyses. We demonstrate that perioperative glucocorticoid regimens may reduce cerebrovascular events and in-stent stenosis in FD-treated patients, warranting randomized trials.

articles.title: Baseline radiographic and microbiologic predictors of treatment outcomes in a shortened all-oral regimen for MDR/RR-TB
articles.titleEn: Baseline radiographic and microbiologic predictors of treatment outcomes in a shortened all-oral regimen for MDR/RR-TB
articles.abstract: WHO-endorsed shortened, all-oral regimens have improved tolerability and outcomes for MDR/RR-TB treatment, but predictors of poor outcomes remain incompletely-characterized. We conducted a prospective cohort study (NCT05871489) of adults with bacteriologically-confirmed pulmonary MDR/RR-TB treated with a shortened, all-oral regimen in Lesotho. We evaluated baseline microbiologic and radiographic features and their associations with time-to-culture-conversion, end-of-treatment outcomes, and final post-treatment outcomes. Among 238 participants (median age 41 [IQR:31–56], 29% female, 62% with HIV), there were 27 unfavorable outcomes (20 deaths, 3 treatment failures, 4 recurrences). 142 of 148 (95.9%) with positive baseline cultures experienced conversion within four months. Fibrosis, cavitation, bilateral disease, and high smear grade were associated with delayed culture conversion and lower odds of treatment success. Bilateral disease was more strongly associated with unfavorable outcomes in those without HIV; fibrosis and high smear grade showed stronger associations among those with HIV. Cavitation with high smear grade (uOR=0.29, 95%CI:0.11–0.78; aOR=0.39, 95%CI:0.14-1.14), and severe fibrocavitary disease (multi-lobar fibrosis and at least one cavity ≥5 cm) (uOR=0.20, 95%CI:0.07–0.64; aOR=0.26, 95%CI:0.07-0.94) were negatively associated with favorable final outcomes. These findings suggest that baseline sputum and chest radiographic features—particularly in-combination—identify higher-risk patients and may inform risk-adapted strategies for shortened all-oral MDR/RR-TB regimens.

articles.title: Nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate hybrid electrolyte for high-voltage lithium batteries via preemptive passivation
articles.titleEn: Nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate hybrid electrolyte for high-voltage lithium batteries via preemptive passivation
articles.abstract: Achieving high energy density without compromising safety remains a significant challenge for advanced batteries. Nonflammable electrolytes can mitigate fire risk, but poor bulk and interfacial properties of such electrolytes limit their application. Here, a nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate electrolyte was developed, achieving a self-extinguishing time of ~0 s and stable cycling in both lithium metal and lithium-ion batteries under high-voltage conditions. The electrolyte comprising lithium hexafluorophosphate dissolved in dimethylsulfamoyl fluoride, fluoroethylene carbonate, and ethyl methyl carbonate at low concentration establishes a weakly solvating environment, wherein dimethylsulfamoyl fluoride and fluoroethylene carbonate preferentially contribute to stabilize the positive and negative electrodes, while working together to enhance the rate capability, low-temperature performance, and long-term cycling at high-voltage. Accelerating rate calorimetry revealed a delayed thermal runaway onset by 87 °C, correlating with Broadness Index. These findings suggest that preemptive passivation on both electrodes, when coupled with nonflammable electrolyte design, can provide a viable route toward safe, high-energy lithium batteries.

articles.title: Satellite‐Based Estimates of Irrigation Water Use Versus Modeling Reconstructions: How Much do They Differ?
articles.titleEn: Satellite‐Based Estimates of Irrigation Water Use Versus Modeling Reconstructions: How Much do They Differ?
articles.abstract: Knowing water amounts destined for agricultural practices, essentially consisting of irrigation water use (IWU), is essential for water resources management. Although explicit and consistent information on IWU is generally lacking worldwide, remote sensing and modeling platforms offer valuable solutions for estimating it. The objective of this work is to perform an intercomparison between satellite‐based IWU products and modeling reconstructions over four main irrigation hotspots worldwide: the Contiguous United States (CONUS), the Ebro basin (Spain), India, and the Murray‐Darling basin (Australia). Remote‐sensing‐based IWU estimated through Soil‐Moisture‐Inversion (SM‐Inversion) and SM‐Delta approaches are considered. As modeled data, five Global Hydrological Models are evaluated: H08, PCR‐GLOBWB, WaterGAP, LPJmL, and QUAlloc. Reference irrigation volumes are exploited to assess which source is more reliable. Over CONUS and Murray‐Darling basin, lower discrepancies between data sources (satellite or modeling) are detected. Referring to spatially‐averaged IWU magnitudes, the comparison over CONUS provides ranging from 9.52 to 12.21 mm/month, between 3.24 and 7.06 mm/month, and Pearson correlation () from 0.77 to 0.90. The same intervals for the Murray‐Darling basin are 8.04–17.70 mm/month for , 4.81–12.63 mm/month for , and 0.42–0.85 for . Consequently, over such areas, similar performances in reproducing actual irrigation amounts by satellite estimates and modeling reconstructions, when available, are found. Over the Ebro basin, where the strongest discrepancies are found, satellite‐based data sets outperform model outputs in reproducing reference data. The lack of in situ observations for India prevents a clear assessment of the results, but insights on differences introduced by parametrizations are established.

articles.title: Alaskan Glaciers in a Warming Climate
articles.titleEn: Alaskan Glaciers in a Warming Climate
articles.abstract: Glaciers across Alaska are undergoing rapid mass loss, with implications for sea‐level rise, natural hazards, water resources, and more. Here, we utilize new snowline and melt extent observations of Alaskan glaciers at high spatiotemporal resolutions to improve projections to 2100. Specifically, we incorporate these observations into the calibration scheme for the large‐scale Python Glacier Evolution Model (PyGEM), and subsequently simulate future changes under various climate scenarios. We estimate that glaciers in Alaska will lose 49 ± 17% to 73 ± 26% of their 2015 mass by the end of the century, depending on the future climate. Nearly all small glaciers ( 2 ) will disappear by 2100 regardless of the climate scenario, along with the smallest glacierized subregions of Alaska, namely, the Brooks and Talkeetna ranges. Across larger subregions, negative mass balance is projected to peak in the middle of the 21st century for the modest future warming scenario (i.e., SSP1‐2.6), while negative mass balance continues to increase to 2100 for the most aggressive future warming scenario (SSP5‐8.5). Much of these changes are attributed to increasing temperatures that cause greater melt in addition to a shift in early‐winter precipitation from snow to rain which reduces accumulation and enhances melt by exposing the underlying ice earlier in the next ablation season. Of the remaining glaciers in 2100, 15%–60%, depending on the future climate, have no accumulation area and are thus committed to disappearance. Overall, the widespread loss of glaciers in Alaska by 2100 has implications on ecology, water resources, natural hazards, and tourism across the region.

articles.title: Investigating Cloud–Radiation Error Compensations Stemming From Climate Model Calibration
articles.titleEn: Investigating Cloud–Radiation Error Compensations Stemming From Climate Model Calibration
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Compensating errors are an obstacle to the development of climate models. We wonder if systematic errors in simulated cloud properties might result from forced error compensation due to targeting top‐of‐atmosphere radiative fluxes in the tuning process while using an inaccurate radiative transfer (RT) parameterization. Here, we investigate the extent to which parametric and structural errors in state‐of‐the‐art RT models might be offset by errors relating to cloud properties, and under what circumstances. For this we run tuning experiments with a Single‐Column version of a climate Model (SCM), with and without a parameterization of 3D radiative effects of clouds, targeting reference solar fluxes calculated on Large‐Eddy Simulation cloud fields. In a first set of tuning experiments, the parameters that control cloud geometry in the radiative transfer code are tuned assuming perfect cloud profiles. Compensation mechanisms are found between cloud geometry effects, notably between cloud vertical overlap and 3D effects. In a second set of experiments, cloud geometry parameters are set to nominal values, and free parameters of the boundary layer and cloud parameterizations are tuned, still targeting radiative metrics. We found that, when 3D effects are neglected in these experiments, reasonable fluxes are obtained only at the expense of overestimated cloud fractions, partly compensating for underestimated cloud reflectivity at low sun. Targeting mean solar‐angle fluxes instead of detailed ones removes this mechanism entirely. This study both enlightens some compensation errors specific to cloud–radiation interaction and illustrates more generally how the tuning tool can be used to study and quantify compensating errors.

articles.title: Rapid coral bleaching recovery via symbiont transfer from healthy corals
articles.titleEn: Rapid coral bleaching recovery via symbiont transfer from healthy corals
articles.abstract: Coral bleaching, the temperature-induced loss of dinoflagellate symbionts, is a major driver of global coral reef decline. Although corals can regain symbionts through repopulation of residual symbionts or via environmental acquisition, these processes are often too slow to prevent coral mortality. Mechanisms that enable rapid and effective symbiont reintroduction leading to full recovery remain largely unknown. Here, we demonstrate coral bleaching recovery through contact-mediated transfer of symbionts from healthy corals using small coral fragments. We show that symbiont transfer is rapid, occurring over days to weeks, and highly efficient, with only brief physical contact with healthy corals required. A single week of contact, and in some cases as few as 3 days, provides sufficient symbionts to initiate sustained and full self-recovery. By 1 week, symbiont population doubling time is approximately 4 days, up to an order of magnitude faster than most recovery times for corals in the field. We identify tissue fusion as the mechanism enabling directional symbiont transfer from healthy to bleached coral tissue. As a result, contact-dependent recovery is restricted to corals of the same genet, whereas heterologous genet pairings trigger antagonistic interactions. However, symbiont transfer via polyp uptake occurs immediately upon contact in both same-genet and mixed-genet pairings, revealing an additional, slower pathway for symbiont transfer that is insufficient on its own to support colony recovery. Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized natural process for efficiently reintroducing symbionts to bleached corals, providing a foundation for research into potential recovery interventions.

articles.title: Climate choices and attention are shaped more by politics than weather
articles.titleEn: Climate choices and attention are shaped more by politics than weather

articles.title: Political affiliation impacts climate attention and choice beyond extreme weather exposure
articles.titleEn: Political affiliation impacts climate attention and choice beyond extreme weather exposure
articles.abstract: Political polarization and increasing exposure to extreme weather can shape public engagement with climate change, yet the underlying psychological mechanisms remain unclear. In this Registered Report, we examine how political affiliation, extreme weather exposure and subjective attribution influence climate-relevant information search and decision-making in a US sample ( N = 1,451). We combined a process-tracing paradigm within an incentivized decision task involving real carbon emissions with objective data on extreme weather exposure. Democrats attended more to carbon emission information and made more pro-climate choices than Republicans, with no evidence of moderation by objective extreme weather exposure. The subjective attribution of extreme weather to climate change was associated with greater attention to carbon information, more pro-climate choices and moderated the effects of exposure on both outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of political affiliation in climate-relevant decision-making and suggest that extreme weather effects depend less on exposure itself than on how these experiences are interpreted.

articles.title: Palaeoclimate constraints narrow uncertainty in future Arctic winter sea ice projections
articles.titleEn: Palaeoclimate constraints narrow uncertainty in future Arctic winter sea ice projections
articles.abstract: Arctic sea ice decline has been observed across all seasons and is projected to continue in the future. Relative to historical observations, climate models show their largest biases and uncertainties during winter, when ice cover strongly regulates air–sea heat exchange, ocean mixing and atmospheric circulation. Palaeoclimate records offer opportunities to evaluate model performance beyond the historical period, but applications have remained largely qualitative. Here we compile an Arctic-wide database of mid-Holocene (5–7 thousand years ago) biomarkers to assess sea ice simulations of this past warm period. Using a recently developed proxy system model, we present a Bayesian palaeoclimate model weighting scheme that refines the multi-model mean winter sea ice extent through fully quantitative proxy-model comparisons, accounting for model interdependence and non-stationary proxy seasonality. We demonstrate that, by adjusting the contribution of each model to the ensemble mean based on proxy evidence, model weights can eliminate biases and reduce uncertainties by 85%, to the level of interannual variability. Weighted projections using the same climate models indicate that future winter sea ice extent may be nearly 1 million km 2 lower than prior estimates across forthcoming decades and possible emissions scenarios, with broad implications for Arctic ecosystems, mid-latitude weather, and cryosphere stability.

articles.title: Thermal imbalance drives avian performance and responses to climate warming
articles.titleEn: Thermal imbalance drives avian performance and responses to climate warming
articles.abstract: Thermal performance curves are widely used to predict ectothermic responses to climate warming but are less effective for predicting endotherm performance across environmental conditions because thermoregulation often decouples body temperature from ambient temperature. We develop theory and provide empirical evidence for performance curves in endotherms structured by net sensible heat flux (Q), an integrative index of thermoregulatory imbalance. Using biophysical simulations in tree swallows, we show that performance varies predictably with Q (which we term “QPCs”), thereby explaining variation in nestling provisioning performance, reproductive fitness, and geographic limits, while also forecasting responses to climate change. We also demonstrate that thermal imbalance helps shape breeding ranges of birds across North America. Our findings introduce Q as a broadly relevant ecophysiological dimension that constrains performance in endotherms and provides a framework for predicting endotherm responses to climate warming.

articles.title: Poly(phenolic) deposition is a prerequisite to poly(aliphatic) deposition for functional potato suberin
articles.titleEn: Poly(phenolic) deposition is a prerequisite to poly(aliphatic) deposition for functional potato suberin
articles.abstract: Suberin deposition in specialized cells is a critical aspect of plant protection, providing both water retention and pathogen protection functions. Tissue specific suberization during plant development is mirrored by its wound induction in cells that do not normally suberize and provides a robust experimental system to investigate the process. Suberized cells are characterized by a cell wall–associated lignin-like poly(phenolic) domain, and an ester-linked poly(aliphatic) domain, with the latter often laid down in distinct lamellar bands between the cell wall and plasma membrane. Previous work provides evidence that poly(phenolic) deposition precedes, and is necessary for, poly(aliphatic) deposition. To test this further, we generated RNAi knockdown lines of three wound-induced peroxidase genes, PRX19, PRX55, and PRX105 , in potato ( Solanum tuberosum ), the tubers of which produce an abundance of suberin upon wounding. Peroxidases catalyze the oxidative free radical coupling of phenolic monomers to form the suberin poly(phenolic) domain. The wound-induced suberin of PRX19-RNAi tubers had severely reduced poly(phenolics), reduced poly(aliphatics), and no apparent lamella. Functionally, wound-induced PRX19-RNAi tubers were more permeable to water loss and susceptible to bacterial soft rot. Overall, our data support the hypothesis that poly(phenolic) domain assembly is a strict requirement for subsequent deposition of aliphatic lamella within wound-induced suberin.

articles.title: AI can persuade people to take political actions
articles.titleEn: AI can persuade people to take political actions
articles.abstract: There is substantial concern about the ability of advanced AI to influence people’s behavior. A rapidly growing body of research has found that AI can produce large persuasive effects on people’s attitudes, but whether AI can persuade people to take consequential real-world actions has remained unclear. In two large preregistered experiments ( N = 17 , 950 responses from 14,779 people), we used conversational AI models to persuade participants on a range of attitudinal and behavioral outcomes, including signing real petitions and donating money to charity. We found sizable AI persuasion effects on these behavioral outcomes (e.g. + 19.7 percentage points on petition signing). However, we observed no evidence of a correlation between AI persuasion effects on attitudes and effects on behavior. Moreover, we replicated prior findings that information provision drove effects on attitudes, but found no such evidence for our behavioral outcomes. In a test of eight behavioral persuasion strategies, the strategy focused on information provision produced the smallest behavioral effect, though differences among the eight were small. Taken together, these results suggest that previous findings relying on attitudinal outcomes may generalize poorly to behavior, and therefore risk substantially mischaracterizing the real-world behavioral impact of AI persuasion.

However, we observed no evidence of a correlation between AI persuasion effects on attitudes and effects on behavior. Moreover, we replicated prior findings that information provision drove effects on attitudes, but found no such evidence for our behavioral outcomes. In a test of eight behavioral persuasion strategies, the strategy focused on information provision produced the smallest behavioral effect, though differences among the eight were small. Taken together, these results suggest that previous findings relying on attitudinal outcomes may generalize poorly to behavior, and therefore risk substantially mischaracterizing the real-world behavioral impact of AI persuasion.

articles.title: Altered sperm DNA methylation provides an epigenetic route from overweight and older men to intergenerational disease transmission
articles.titleEn: Altered sperm DNA methylation provides an epigenetic route from overweight and older men to intergenerational disease transmission
articles.abstract: The occurrence of childhood neurodevelopmental disorders has been steadily increasing for decades, yet we have little understanding of modes of inheritance implicated in these diseases. Epidemiology studies have revealed an association between an elevated paternal Body Mass Index (BMI) and age as factors implicated in increased risk for neurodevelopmental disorders in children. Epigenetic regulation of gene expression by DNA methylation at cytosines is susceptible to environmental, diet, and lifestyle changes. Yet, whether a man’s BMI and age influence the sperm methylome and potentially impact offspring development remains unresolved. Using MethylC capture sequencing, we identified over 38,000 differentially methylated CpGs in the sperm of men with an elevated BMI, with overlap occurring in regions associated with advanced paternal age. These were enriched for neural gene and disease ontologies. Differentially methylated regions localized to transposable elements that can act as active enhancers during human zygotic genome activation, and at gene promoters for early lineage specification. These results suggest that sperm methylome alterations that are linked to an elevated BMI may influence key embryonic transcriptional processes, notably those associated with trophectoderm and placental development.

articles.title: Nuclear BbAtg8 interacts with BbMac1 as a transcriptional modulator to sustain nuclear copper homeostasis during conidial germination
articles.titleEn: Nuclear BbAtg8 interacts with BbMac1 as a transcriptional modulator to sustain nuclear copper homeostasis during conidial germination
articles.abstract: Pathogenic fungi endure host impose copper starvation by tightly coordinating trace metal homeostasis. However, how pathogens synchronize endogenous metal recycling with exogenous copper uptake to promote infection remains enigmatic. Using the entomopathogenic fungus Beauveria bassiana , we uncovered a synergistic regulatory network that prioritizes nuclear copper enrichment during conidial germination. Under copper deprivation, the fungus deploys a highly coordinated dual-track survival strategy. In the cytoplasm, the core autophagy protein BbAtg8 drives autophagic flux, specifically triggering mitophagy to degrade mitochondria, thereby promoting the turnover and mobilization of endogenous copper stores. Concurrently, a nonlipidated pool of BbAtg8 translocates to the nucleus to coordinate exogenous uptake. Within the nucleus, BbAtg8 directly interacts with the copper-fist transcription factor BbMac1 via a functional Atg8-interacting motif (AIM). This physical interaction serves as a potent transcriptional modulator, significantly enhancing BbMac1’s DNA-binding affinity. Consequently, the Atg8-Mac1 complex hyper-activates the expression of three functionally redundant copper transporters (BbCtr1, BbCtr2, and BbCtr4) to aggressively absorb extracellular copper. Strikingly, severe copper deprivation triggers a dynamic spatial enrichment of these classical copper transporters at the nuclear envelope, which correlates with the sustained maintenance of nuclear copper homeostasis required for essential genomic functions and full fungal virulence. Together, these findings reveal how pathogens synchronize mitophagy-mediated endogenous turnover with Mac1-driven exogenous uptake, fundamentally expanding the role of autophagy proteins BbAtg8 into direct transcriptional coordinators of metal homeostasis. This dual-track regulatory model not only deepens our understanding of fungal adaptation to nutritional immunity but also provides potential targets for disrupting copper homeostasis to control fungal pathogens.

articles.title: Physical origins of speed control in swimming fishes
articles.titleEn: Physical origins of speed control in swimming fishes
articles.abstract: The linear relationship between tail-beat frequency and swimming speed in fish, first described by Bainbridge in 1958, has since been confirmed in species as disparate as eels and tuna. Dimensional scaling has explained why linearity should emerge at high Reynolds numbers, but the frequency–speed relationship itself has remained empirical, with no physical framework describing its behavior across swimming regimes, and no account of what sets the two quantities that define it: the distance covered per tail beat and the frequency below which forward motion supposedly ceases. Here, we derive a relationship from a balance of fin thrust, generated by a leading-edge vortex, and drag due to the boundary layer on the body. This framework yields an explicit expression for speed in terms of midline kinematics and body morphology. This formulation shows that the maximum stride length is set by the undulatory wavelength and the tail-beat phase offset, rather than by the conventional scaling metric of body length, and that no minimum frequency is required for forward motion. The model reproduces kinematic measurements from freely swimming glass catfish, published simulations, and Bainbridge’s original data. Without recalibration, it predicts the results of independent simulations spanning wide variations in wavelength, phase offset, and morphology to within ten percent. Linear scaling is thus one asymptotic limit of a more general propulsive relationship linking morphology and body-wave kinematics to swimming speed in fishes and bioinspired vehicles, where the body waveform, rather than the actuation frequency, emerges as the variable that sets performance.

articles.title: Global origins of tuna and billfish fisheries reveal the transition from coastal access to oceanic exploitation
articles.titleEn: Global origins of tuna and billfish fisheries reveal the transition from coastal access to oceanic exploitation
articles.abstract: Ocean ecosystems have played a crucial role in people’s lives around the world for millennia. However, questions persist about when, why, and how people first began removing biomass from offshore habitats and established fisheries in distant, oceanic environments. We explore the antiquity and evolution of tuna (Thunnini) and billfish (Istiophoridae/Xiphiidae) fisheries, two groups of fishes that occur around the world, are economically significant, and are ecologically important open ocean apex predators. The earliest archaeological evidence of fishing for tuna occurs ~44,000 years ago and billfish at ~10,000 years ago, with early fisheries for some tuna species appearing around the world by 3,000 to 1,000 years ago. Most early fisheries are in areas where tunas and billfishes could be accessed relatively close to shore (e.g., submarine canyons) and/or where these fishes may come inshore seasonally or during warm ocean events. Early tuna and billfish fisheries were often linked to ceremony/ritual, alongside advances in maritime technologies. With few exceptions, sustained and intensive commercial exploitation of pelagic predators in offshore and oceanic habitats is a late development in the human past, occurring primarily during the last 200 y. Our findings document a long-term continuum of human interactions with global marine ecosystems spanning thousands of years, including significant differences between the timing and pathways by which people became dominant ecological drivers in nearshore compared to offshore/oceanic ecosystems.

articles.title: PCS-UQ: Uncertainty quantification via the Predictability–Computability–Stability framework
articles.titleEn: PCS-UQ: Uncertainty quantification via the Predictability–Computability–Stability framework
articles.abstract: As machine learning (ML) enters high-stakes domains, trustworthy uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for safety. In this paper we introduce PCS-UQ, a framework based on the predictability, computability, and stability (PCS) principles for veridical data science. Starting with a candidate set of models or algorithms, PCS-UQ integrates a rigorous prediction-check to screen out unsuitable models in the set and utilizes bootstrap samples in order to capture both inter-sample variability and algorithmic instability for the prediction-checked algorithms. We then introduce a multiplicative calibration scheme to enhance local adaptivity, which can be viewed as a score function in conformal prediction. Moreover, we produce a compilation of 17 real-world regression datasets with manually constructed subgroups. On this benchmark, PCS-UQ maintains the target coverage while outperforming or matching conformal methods equipped with oracle-selected algorithms in interval width. PCS-UQ achieves consistent subgroup coverage, outperforming these oracle-selected conformal methods. Notably, PCS-UQ stands out in achieving both competitive interval widths and consistent subgroup coverage. Across six classification datasets, PCS-UQ reduces prediction set sizes by 20%. To scale the framework for deep learning, we propose computationally efficient variants that bypass expensive retraining. On three computer vision benchmarks, these variants reduce prediction set sizes by 20% over conformal baselines. Finally, we provide a theoretical proof that a modified PCS-UQ algorithm preserves valid coverage under exchangeability as a form of split conformal inference.

articles.title: Controlled functionalization of cellulose nanocrystals directs polymer-specific protein coronas and immune cell interactions
articles.titleEn: Controlled functionalization of cellulose nanocrystals directs polymer-specific protein coronas and immune cell interactions
articles.abstract: Polymer coatings are widely used to suppress nonspecific protein adsorption and modulate nanoparticle–cell interactions. However, the biological outcomes of polymer-functionalized nanoparticles remain difficult to predict in complex biological environments because protein corona formation rapidly alters nanoparticle identity. This challenge is particularly pronounced when hydrophobic moieties are incorporated for imaging or therapeutic applications, as they can promote nonspecific interactions at the nano–bio interface. Herein, we establish a modular grafting-to platform based on cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) that enables systematic comparison of polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based, zwitterionic, and acrylamide-based polymers with controlled grafting density and chain conformation on a common porphyrin-modified surface. We demonstrate that dense polymer brushes reduce nonspecific protein adsorption in single-protein assays. By contrast, all CNC surfaces form dynamic coronas upon exposure to serum proteins, while specific polymer coatings selectively enrich or suppress distinct protein populations. We further demonstrate that polymer-dependent immune cell interactions are substantially reduced following protein corona formation, although differences among polymer chemistries persist. Zwitterionic coatings broadly suppress immune cell interactions, whereas PEG-based coatings preferentially promote interactions with antigen-presenting cells. These findings establish design principles for polymer-functionalized nanoparticles with specific immune cell interaction profiles.

articles.title: Systemic collapse emergence from climate-induced perturbations in transportation networks
articles.titleEn: Systemic collapse emergence from climate-induced perturbations in transportation networks
articles.abstract: The interaction between human infrastructures and external events results in loss of functionality or even complete system disruption through a snowball effect of cascading failures. Their complex interplay challenges their prevention, affecting the human population that rely on their functionality. Understanding how these networks respond to external perturbations is crucial for predicting and mitigating the impacts of disruptive events. In particular, meteorological events, while not preventable, can have significant impacts on human infrastructure. Here, we propose a model coupling the dynamics of transportation systems to the dynamics of external events considered as fields, to capture at the same time the critical behavior of the former and the level of influence of the latter. The impact of rainfalls on real-world railway networks provides a compelling case study, showcasing local endemic and system-wide disruptions above a critical value of the rainfall strength. Remarkably, localized perturbations on the wider network reveals the local weaknesses of the global infrastructure, and we assess them in terms of system perturbability and corresponding societal risk. Our framework opens the door to the quantitative analysis of criticalities in essential human infrastructure imputable to vulnerabilities that are set to intensify due to climate change.

articles.title: Big Data for Small Streams: Leveraging a Coarse National Model to Enhance Fine‐Resolution Stream Temperature Predictions
articles.titleEn: Big Data for Small Streams: Leveraging a Coarse National Model to Enhance Fine‐Resolution Stream Temperature Predictions
articles.abstract: Predictive stream temperature models are commonly used to address spatial and temporal gaps in observational data because stream temperature information is essential for environmental management decisions. National models capture broad patterns driven by climate, topography, and seasonality, but often lack the spatial resolution to simulate fine‐scale variation in groundwater discharge, riparian shading, or tributary inflows. In contrast, watershed models may simulate finer‐resolution patterns but miss regional drivers or be limited by scarcity of observations. To generate watershed‐extent, fine‐resolution stream temperature predictions, we developed 18 multiscale machine‐learning models that leverage (a) a broad‐extent, coarse‐resolution stream temperature model and (b) finer‐resolution observations and predictor data. The coarse‐resolution model simulates daily stream temperature across the conterminous United States on the National Hydrologic Geospatial Fabric (13.7 km median reach length; 865,364 km total). The fine‐resolution models simulate daily stream temperature on the National Hydrography Dataset Plus version 2 (1.5 km median; 5,192,808 km total). We compared multiscale models to seven purely broad‐ (national) or watershed‐extent models, testing them in eight watersheds (436–985 km 2 ) with differing hydrologic settings and under realistic data availability scenarios. Especially when observations within a watershed were scarce, multiscale models generated more accurate predictions than national or watershed‐specific models. A recurrent graph convolution neural network pretrained on coarse predictions and fine‐tuned on watershed‐specific observations was most accurate across watersheds and data scenarios. These results highlight that leveraging both coarse, national results and watershed‐specific data can increase model accuracies, particularly when observations within a watershed are spatially or temporally limited.

articles.title: How Hydrological Structural Connectivity Controls Red Soil Erosion During Multiple‐Intermittent Rainfalls
articles.titleEn: How Hydrological Structural Connectivity Controls Red Soil Erosion During Multiple‐Intermittent Rainfalls
articles.abstract: Hydrological structural connectivity is key to regulating hillslope erosion, but its formation and interactions with runoff‐sediment dynamics during intermittent rainfall remain unclear. Through simulated intermittent rainfall (three consecutive rainfall events with a 1‐day interval between each, intensities: 30, 60, 90 mm hr −1 ) combined with overland‐flow hydraulics measurements and high‐resolution UAV photogrammetry, this study reveals how hydrological structural connectivity dynamically controls erosion. Runoff‐sediment responses showed strong intensity dependence. At 30 mm hr −1 the runoff coefficient rose continuously, whereas under higher intensities it increased and then stabilized. Soil loss rates rose steadily at low intensity, followed a “rise‐then‐fall” pattern at medium intensity, and declined at high intensity. Connectivity strengthened with rainfall progression, but its growth rate declined as intensity increased. The key structural connectivity index |RF| rose with intensity (36.71, 39.36, 41.52 under 30, 60, 90 mm hr −1 , respectively; ×10 −6 ), while its growth rate decreases significantly (18.58%, 9.96%, 1.02%), showing earlier stabilization under high intensity. |RF| exhibits significant positive correlations with surface runoff, hydrodynamic parameters, and key rill morphological parameters, indicating that connectivity influences erosion processes by regulating flow pathways and convergence efficiency. Under low rainfall intensity, erosion promotes connectivity development, whereas under high rainfall intensity, an early‐established highly connected network constrains further erosion. As rainfall intensity increased, the erosion system shifts gradually from an “erosion‐driven connectivity development” regime to a “connectivity‐controlled erosion regulation” regime. This study reveals the nonlinear responses of hillslope erosion from a connectivity perspective, offering a theoretical basis for mechanism understanding and targeted conservation strategies.

articles.title: High Frequency Storm Sampling and Analysis of Hysteretic Transport Behavior Offers Insights Into Dynamic Microplastic Activation, Flux and Depletion Within a Peri‐Urban Stream
articles.titleEn: High Frequency Storm Sampling and Analysis of Hysteretic Transport Behavior Offers Insights Into Dynamic Microplastic Activation, Flux and Depletion Within a Peri‐Urban Stream
articles.abstract: Previous research has pinpointed storm events as significant potential controls of microplastic (MP) export to the oceans. Hysteretic behavior of discharge ( Q )—concentration (c) relationships for suspended sediment (SS) and solutes has been found important in understanding the dynamic activation and transport of these substances, additionally providing better estimations of long‐term loads. Due to limited availability of high frequency event‐based MP concentration data their potential hysteretic behavior has not been studied, leaving a substantial knowledge gap regarding the fate and transport mechanisms controlling MP activation and retention within catchments. We pioneer the use of high frequency MP data collected during a storm event revealing the time variable activation of different sources and transport mechanisms within a peri‐urban catchment. Surface water samples were collected before, during and after the event and combined with discharge and turbidity data to quantify MP concentrations and fluxes. Analysis of the hysteretic behavior of the Q‐c relationship revealed a clockwise hysteresis pattern with MP concentration peaking before Q , suggesting potential MP supply limitation for the sampled event. Regression analysis indicates Q to be the primary driving force promoting MP flux, with strong correlations between Q and MP concentration in rising and falling limbs. A strong Q ‐ turbidity relationship was observed only in the rising limb, potentially indicating spatial differences in the sources of SS and MPs transported in the falling limb. Total MP flux increased by 17–217 times to that of baseflow, highlighting the significance of often‐overlooked dynamics when calculating yearly MP flux.

articles.title: Time‐Varying Operation Policies With GRU‐Based Parameterization for Adaptive Multi‐Objective Reservoir Operation Under Climate Change
articles.titleEn: Time‐Varying Operation Policies With GRU‐Based Parameterization for Adaptive Multi‐Objective Reservoir Operation Under Climate Change
articles.abstract: Designing reservoir operation policies that can adapt to non‐stationary hydroclimatic conditions is a major challenge for water resources management under climate change. This study develops an adaptive dynamic operation policy (ADOP), in which Gaussian radial basis functions (RBFs) are coupled with a gated recurrent unit (GRU)‐based parameterization module that maps meteorological information to time‐varying RBF weights. Using the reservoir system in the Qingjiang River Basin, China, as a case study, ADOP is optimized using an expanded historical hydroclimatic ensemble within an evolutionary multi‐objective direct policy search (EMODPS) framework and is evaluated under both an independent historical test period and 12 GCM‐based climate scenarios. A static operation policy (SOP) and a scenario‐specific re‐optimized ideal operation policy (IOP) are used as benchmarks. Results show that ADOP outperforms SOP under both historical training and test conditions. Under future scenarios, ADOP achieves higher hypervolume than SOP in 10 of 12 scenarios, indicating the advantage of the time‐varying parameterization in out‐of‐sample conditions. Although both historically trained policies retain a performance gap relative to the re‐optimized IOP, ADOP partially mitigates this gap. The water‐level and release trajectories for representative years further demonstrate that the advantage of ADOP is associated with improved storage–release coordination. Moreover, a diagnostic comparison supports the value of the GRU‐based module, as adding meteorological inputs to a static RBF policy does not reproduce ADOP's gains. The proposed time‐varying policy provides a practical pathway for improving the adaptability of historically trained reservoir operation policies under uncertain future hydroclimatic conditions.

articles.title: Impact of Global Warming‐Induced Sea‐Surface Salt Concentration Changes on Island Groundwater System
articles.titleEn: Impact of Global Warming‐Induced Sea‐Surface Salt Concentration Changes on Island Groundwater System
articles.abstract: Global warming is altering sea‐surface salt concentration (SSC) through intensified evaporation, shifted precipitation patterns, and accelerated melting of polar ice. Subsurface freshwater in oceanic islands is typically shaped like a thin lens due to limited land area and recharge, often the primary freshwater source for local communities and highly vulnerable to seawater intrusion (SWI). However, the effects of SSC changes on freshwater lens (FWL) and SWI extent in island aquifers remain unknown, and there is little knowledge on how hydraulic conductivity (HK), local aquifer recharge (RCH) and island width ( L ) affect these effects. To end this, this study employs a simplified two‐dimensional, variable‐density island groundwater simulation model to investigate how SSC affects FWL and SWI extent across seven distinct hydrogeological scenarios, using six quantitative indicators: relative changes in (a) average water table elevation (WTE), (b) maximum WTE, (c) FWL depth, (d) FWL thickness, (e) fresh groundwater volume, (f) aquifer salt mass. Simulation results demonstrate that rising SSC increases aquifer salt mass and elevates WTE while shrinking FWL (reducing its depth, thickness, and freshwater volume), as enhanced freshwater‐saltwater density contrasts drive more vertical flow pushing FWL upward. Island aquifers with higher HK, lower RCH, or smaller L show minimal changes in WTE and aquifer salt mass but are more sensitive to SSC changes in terms of FWL depth, thickness and fresh groundwater volume. Moreover, WTE and FWL characteristics show greater sensitivity to SSC declines than to SSC increases.

articles.title: The need for uncertainty: why probabilistic LSTMs are key to improving flood predictions and enabling learned warning rules
articles.titleEn: The need for uncertainty: why probabilistic LSTMs are key to improving flood predictions and enabling learned warning rules
articles.abstract: Deterministic model predictions can struggle to adequately capture extreme events such as floods and droughts, which are of particular importance in hydrology. This limitation arises because deterministic models collapse the conditional discharge distribution to a single point estimate. Probabilistic modeling provides a way to address this issue by explicitly representing uncertainty and assigning non-zero probabilities to all possible outcomes, including extreme events, thereby capturing the entire conditional discharge distribution. Motivated by this perspective, we examine whether probabilistic Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models improve the representation of extreme events in rainfall–runoff simulations across Switzerland. The differing degree of flexibility in the models leads to different degrees and distinct patterns of miscalibration in the predictive distributions. For the extreme discharges (top 0.05 % of the marginal discharge distribution), the deterministic LSTM systematically underestimates 97 % of these events, whereas 83 % of these fall within the probabilistic model's 99th percentile prediction interval. Given the rarity of these events, representing them as outcomes near the upper tail of the predictive distribution is both expected and statistically consistent. Building on the additional information provided by probabilistic runoff predictions, we further show how they can be translated into actionable flood warnings using reinforcement learning. To this end, we introduce a Flood Risk Communication Agent (FRiCA) that operates on probabilistic runoff predictions and learns risk-aware decision rules for issuing warnings of varying intensity. Results indicate that the FRiCA outperforms simple fixed heuristics, such as issuing warnings based on the deterministic LSTM predictions or a fixed high quantile (e.g., the 99th percentile). The learnt behavior demonstrates the potential of reinforcement learning as a decision layer for improved flood risk communication, and motivates further exploration of better reward design and policy network optimization for context-dependent decision policies that adapt to varying hydrological and societal contexts.

articles.title: Meso-NH-ISO v1.0: a water stable isotopologue scheme in the non-hydrostatic mesoscale atmospheric model Meso-NH – application to a 2D West African squall line
articles.titleEn: Meso-NH-ISO v1.0: a water stable isotopologue scheme in the non-hydrostatic mesoscale atmospheric model Meso-NH – application to a 2D West African squall line
articles.abstract: Better understanding how convective processes impact the isotopic composition of atmospheric water has implications for understanding phenomena such as squall lines or tropical cyclones, and for reconstructions of past rainfall extreme events. With this motivation, we implemented water stable isotopologues (HD 16 O and H218O) in the non-hydrostatic mesoscale atmospheric model Meso-NH and its one-moment bulk mixed-phase microphysics scheme. The water stable isotopologues are subject to the same dynamical and physical processes as the light water, but undergo isotopic fractionation during water phase changes. Both equilibrium and kinetic fractionation processes that occur during water phase changes involving water vapor are taken into account. The implementation is validated on a test case of a 2D simulation of a tropical squall line observed in June 1981 during the COPT 81 field campaign in the Sahel region. The isotopic version of Meso-NH (Meso-NH-ISO) captures the expected evolution of the isotopic composition of both precipitation and water vapor along the squall line. This work opens the door to future isotopic studies using realistic cases of mesoscale convective systems (squall lines, tropical cyclones).

articles.title: Airborne measurements of turbulence and cloud microphysics during PaCE 2022 using the Advanced Max Planck CloudKite Instrument (MPCK + )
articles.titleEn: Airborne measurements of turbulence and cloud microphysics during PaCE 2022 using the Advanced Max Planck CloudKite Instrument (MPCK + )
articles.abstract: This paper presents the data set collected with the Advanced Max Planck CloudKite instrument (MPCK + ) during the Pallas Cloud Experiment (PaCE), conducted at Pallas, Finland, between 19 and 26 September 2022. The data set includes measurements of turbulence, wind shear, and cloud microphysics in the cloudy planetary boundary layer between 0 and 1200 m above ground with flight durations between 1.5 and 3 h. This data set is intended for researchers studying microphysics of boundary layer clouds in the sub-arctic at temperatures above freezing level, providing high-resolution airborne measurements of meteorological variables together with cloud droplet concentration and size distribution data. In particular, the high spatial resolution of less than 10 m between two cloud droplet size distribution samples, the low altitude and the long flight time allow unprecedented insights into stratocumulus and cumulus clouds. The aim of this paper is to describe the data collection process, the structure of the data set, and guidelines for potential users. The data set is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15700506 (Bagheri et al., 2025a) in NetCDF format.

articles.title: Direct and Trait‐Mediated Effects of Climate on Grassland Productivity Across the Alps
articles.titleEn: Direct and Trait‐Mediated Effects of Climate on Grassland Productivity Across the Alps
articles.abstract: Understanding how climate shapes ecosystem productivity through energetic constraints and changes in the functional properties expressed by vegetation remains challenging. This is central to trait‐based biodiversity–ecosystem functioning research in mountain grasslands where warming and environmental gradients interact. Here, we distinguish direct climatic controls on productivity from indirect pathways operating through changes in canopy functional composition, physiological state, and within‐plot spectral functional heterogeneity across the European Alps. Using Sentinel‐2 time series (2017–2024), we quantified canopy functional structure from spectral proxies of pigment investment and water status, within‐plot spectral functional heterogeneity using the functional richness (FRic) metric, and vegetation productivity using near‐infrared reflectance of vegetation (NIRv). We combined panel‐data models with piecewise structural equation modeling to partition climate associations into direct and trait‐mediated components operating through canopy functional properties and used varying‐coefficient models to evaluate how these pathways vary along environmental gradients. We identified two pathways linking climate to productivity. Warmer growing seasons increased productivity directly but were associated with a lower chlorophyll‐to‐carotenoid pigment balance, consistent with greater relative carotenoid investment, generating an opposing indirect pathway. Greater winter snow accumulation reduced productivity primarily through a direct pathway, while its canopy‐mediated pathways were uncertain. Climatic water deficit reduced canopy water status and within‐plot spectral functional heterogeneity, but its direct and total associations with productivity were not distinguishable from zero. Environmental context modulated climate–vegetation relationships. Baseline temperature and moisture availability strongly shaped climate effects on canopy traits and productivity, whereas canopy‐property–productivity relationships varied little across space. Positive productivity responses to warming were stronger in wetter and more seasonally variable climatic contexts, but weakened where baseline winter snow accumulation was greater. Together, our findings show that short‐term productivity responses in mountain grasslands reflect a balance between direct energetic constraints and indirect pathways through integrated canopy functional properties, and that this balance varies along macroclimatic gradients.

articles.title: Tracking crop evapotranspiration and water stress across seasons using multi-sensor UAV observations
articles.titleEn: Tracking crop evapotranspiration and water stress across seasons using multi-sensor UAV observations
articles.abstract: Accurate estimation of crop evapotranspiration (ET) requires resolving how canopy structure and physiological activity regulate land–atmosphere energy exchange. This study applies the Priestley–Taylor Two-Source Energy Balance (TSEB-PT) model using very-high-resolution UAV multi-sensor observations (∼ 15 cm) to estimate ET over a 10 ha field across three seasons (sugar beet, potato, winter wheat). Thermal infrared data provided land surface temperature (LST), while multispectral (MS) and LiDAR data were used to characterize canopy properties, including a fusion-based estimate of the fraction of LAI that is green ( f g ) from MS-derived green area index (GAI) and LiDAR-derived plant area index (PAI). Results showed strong sensitivity to LST, highlighting the importance of thermal calibration, and demonstrated that while GAI and PAI performed similarly during peak growth, GAI better captured functional decline during stress and senescence, particularly in dense canopies. Incorporating dynamic f g improved ET estimates across crops and conditions. Modeled instantaneous ET showed good agreement with eddy covariance (EC) measurements, with RMSE ranging from 0.08 mm h −1 to 0.31 mm h −1 and R 2 values from 0.28 to 0.97 (highest performance excluding senescence). High-resolution UAV-derived LST data and TSEB-PT modeling also enabled early detection of spatial stress patterns not captured by UAV structural or spectral metrics alone. Upscaling instantaneous ET using a reference ET fraction approach produced daily ET estimates with RMSE ranging from 0.96 to 2.30 mm d −1 and R 2 ranging from 0.27 to 0.80 across crops, with improved consistency under energy-balance–closed EC conditions. These daily estimates also enabled assessment of potential crop water stress when compared relative to atmospheric demand (ET RAD = ET / ET 0 ) and improved delineation of sub-field variability compared to coarser-resolution methods. These findings demonstrate the value of integrating UAV multi-sensor data with TSEB-PT for robust, high-resolution ET monitoring and practical applications in precision irrigation and water management.

articles.title: Review article: Mountain flash floods: from hazard formation to disaster risk reduction pathways
articles.titleEn: Review article: Mountain flash floods: from hazard formation to disaster risk reduction pathways
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Mountain flash floods pose growing risks under climate and environmental change, yet cross-regional understanding of their triggering mechanisms, cascading impacts and governance remains fragmented. This review synthesises 1967 studies published during 2000–2025 using bibliometric and topic analyses with qualitative synthesis. By integrating these approaches, we reveal pronounced geographical and thematic imbalances, with research concentrated in Europe and Asia. Flash-flood initiation and impacts are strongly state-dependent, emerging from interactions among storm intensity, duration and spatial concentration, antecedent hydrological conditions, surface controls, and hillslope–channel connectivity. These interactions limit the transferability of fixed rainfall thresholds and support dynamic, multi-source early-warning approaches. The review further shows how hazards are transformed into disaster risk through exposure, vulnerability and capacity conditions, leading to realised economic, social and ecological impacts and cascading disasters. Evidence across non-structural, structural and Nature-Based measures indicates that effective risk reduction requires coordinated portfolios rather than isolated interventions. We develop an adaptive governance framework integrating prevention of new risk, reduction of existing risk and management of residual risk, while addressing exceedance uncertainty, warning-to-action effectiveness, and long-term costs and trade-offs. Overall, this synthesis provides a cross-regional basis for more effective mountain flash-flood risk reduction across mountain regions facing uneven evidence and response capacities worldwide.

articles.title: Temporary carbon storage can mitigate slow-responding climate changes
articles.titleEn: Temporary carbon storage can mitigate slow-responding climate changes
articles.abstract: Carbon removal and storage is central to many net-zero commitments, yet its durability, particularly for nature-based methods, is uncertain due to disturbance risks. Previous work shows that carbon storage-years (the time-integrated quantity of carbon storage) are proportional to time-integrated avoided warming, which in turn causes avoided changes in slow-responding climate variables. Here, we show that temporary carbon storage results in avoided changes in inertial climate variables. Avoided changes in 2100 are proportional to carbon storage-years across a range of storage amounts and emissions scenarios for permafrost carbon, ocean carbon, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, ocean temperature, and thermosteric sea-level rise. By 2300, proportionality persists in some variables, notably sea-level rise, ocean temperature, and ocean carbon. Temporary storage therefore has climate benefits that extend beyond the duration of the storage, with some persistence of benefits even on multi-century timescales. We find that these climate benefits are greatest when temporary storage is paired with ambitious mitigation.

articles.title: A genetically encoded local learning rule enables physical learning in engineered bacteria
articles.titleEn: A genetically encoded local learning rule enables physical learning in engineered bacteria
articles.abstract: Training physical neural networks directly in matter remains difficult because most platforms do not store and update weights within the same physical substrate. Here we show that engineered Escherichia coli can implement a genetically encoded local learning rule acting on persistent biological memory. We introduce memregulons: bacterial memory elements in which coupled plasmids store an analogue weight as the relative abundance of P1 within the P1 + P2 plasmid pool. Environmental inputs activate local promoters, and a shared sublethal kanamycin signal converts promoter activity into differential growth that lowers the stored P1 fraction. Across single-strain trajectories, combined plate-reader and flow-cytometry measurements are consistent with activity- and variance-dependent weight change. At the single-cell level, repeated negative learning reshapes the stored weight distribution as it approaches the lower boundary. In mixed populations and co-cultures, one shared negative learning signal selectively rewrites active memregulons, enabling externally routed supervised tic-tac-toe lessons. We then generalise the architecture across orthogonal chemical inputs and combinatorial promoters, and combine measured co-culture updates with external game analysis and simulate negative pruning in nonlinear-classifier architectures. These results establish physical learning in living matter through local negative updates of genetically encoded analogue weights.

articles.title: MxB N-terminus adopts a stable α-helix to engage the HIV-1 capsid trimer interface
articles.titleEn: MxB N-terminus adopts a stable α-helix to engage the HIV-1 capsid trimer interface
articles.abstract: The HIV-1 capsid, composed of capsid (CA) proteins arranged into a conical surface lattice, serves as a critical platform for host–pathogen interactions. Many host cofactors regulate HIV-1 infection by selectively recognizing the higher-order CA lattice rather than individual monomers or capsomers. Among these, Myxovirus resistance protein B (MxB) is a key cellular restriction factor that binds the capsid via its N-terminal fragment containing an arginine-rich motif (RRR), blocking HIV-1 infection at early infection stages. However, the structural basis of this interaction has remained elusive. Here, we present a structural characterization of the CA lattice in complex with the MxB N-terminal fragment using cryo-electron tomography and subtomogram averaging. Combining cryoEM structures with EM-guided all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, we identify residue-specific interactions between MxB and the CA trimer interfaces. Notably, residues 10-20 of the MxB N-terminus adopt an α-helical conformation that stabilizes binding at the CA trimer interface, revealing a distinct mode of capsid engagement. These findings provide insight into arginine-rich motif–mediated recognition by MxB and other host factors and establish a structural framework for the development of capsid-targeting antiviral therapeutics.

articles.title: Survival and divergence of Arctic endemic cod species during 50,000 years of climate change
articles.titleEn: Survival and divergence of Arctic endemic cod species during 50,000 years of climate change
articles.abstract: Despite significant climate variability in the Northern Hemisphere ~50,000–12,000 years ago, the potential for vertebrates to periodically thrive in the glacial Arctic Ocean has been largely overlooked because ecosystem productivity was assumed to be too low. Here, we analyze fish otoliths preserved in deep-sea sediments and find that two Arctic endemic cod species, ice cod ( Arctogadus glacialis ) and polar cod ( Boreogadus saida ), lived at 87–89 °N ~ 48,000–35,000 years ago and reappeared at the onset of the Holocene ~12,000 years ago. A. glacialis also occurred north of Greenland at 84–85 °N ~ 20,000 years ago, during the peak of the Last Glacial Maximum, suggesting the presence of refugia that enabled survival and divergence from B. saida under the harshest climate conditions. These findings suggest that the glacial Arctic Ocean was not a barren ice desert but rather a breeding ground for the evolution of cold adaptation in marine fish.

articles.title: Multifunctional submicron-scale porous water-foamed cementitious materials
articles.titleEn: Multifunctional submicron-scale porous water-foamed cementitious materials
articles.abstract: Conventional cement-based materials face a fundamental trade-off between low density and high performance, owing to their limited ability to precisely control pore structure. We use ultrasound carbonation to tailor the water distribution and confinement within the flocculation structure, thereby directing product nucleation and growth, and ultimately yielding a multifunctional submicron-scale water-foamed cementitious material. The matrix exhibits a highly refined pore network, 96.8% of which is smaller than 200 nm. The specific compressive strength is 22.5 kN·m·kg −1 , representing an increase of up to 162% relative to a laboratory-prepared foamed concrete control. Simultaneously, the sound transmission loss increases by 131.8% and 107.0% at 2000 Hz and 4000 Hz, respectively, while cumulative CO 2 uptake reaches 7.11% per unit mass of cement after 28 days. The approach relies solely on cement and water as raw materials, reducing process complexity and showing potential for production.

articles.title: Mitochondrial carbonic anhydrase–VB inhibition rescues brain endothelial stress and memory in Alzheimer’s disease models
articles.titleEn: Mitochondrial carbonic anhydrase–VB inhibition rescues brain endothelial stress and memory in Alzheimer’s disease models
articles.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder with no effective cure, characterized by the cerebral parenchymal and vascular accumulation of aggregated amyloid-β (Aβ) and hyperphosphorylated tau. Cerebrovascular and mitochondria dysfunction are early causal events in the progression of AD. Previous studies support that inhibiting carbonic anhydrases (CAs) may prevent mitochondrial and cerebrovascular dysfunction in AD models. Here, we selectively target the mitochondrial CA isoform CA-VB by pharmacological and genetic manipulation in human cerebral microvascular endothelial cells (hCMEC), and we confirm the protective effects of the CA-V inhibitor in AD mice. CA-V inhibition and CA-VB KO prevent Aβ induced mitochondria-mediated endothelial apoptosis, loss of barrier resistance, and hCMEC inflammatory activation. Strikingly, CA-V inhibition also mitigates caspase activation and endothelial cell activation in the brains of 3xTg AD mice, resulting in preserved memory function. Our results demonstrate that selective CA-V inhibition is an effective and promising strategy against AD-mediated cerebrovascular pathology, neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment.

articles.title: Global conservation additionality hindered by persisting fishing pressure in marine protected areas
articles.titleEn: Global conservation additionality hindered by persisting fishing pressure in marine protected areas
articles.abstract: Marine protected areas (MPAs) are the cornerstone of global marine conservation strategies. Yet, their capacity to achieve conservation gains (i.e., conservation additionality) hinges on the decrease in human threats to biodiversity within their boundary, a feature rarely measured or reported. Here, we test a central but underexamined question in global conservation policy: Have MPA implementations actually reduced within-boundary fishing pressure, currently the main direct human threat to marine biodiversity? Using a stratified before-after-control-impact approach, we investigated 861 MPAs of varying levels of protection across all ocean basins, representing half of global MPA coverage, and found that most implementations were not followed by decreases in industrial fishing effort. Protection levels strongly predicted the direction and magnitude of relative changes in fishing effort after implementation. Only fully protected areas were associated with significant decreases in fishing effort within boundaries. Highly protected areas were only associated with lower rates of increase in fishing effort within compared to outside boundaries. Both fully and highly protected areas were implemented in areas experiencing initial low fishing effort, reducing the overall abatement in fishing effort achieved. Conversely, areas with higher initial fishing effort tended to be attributed to MPAs with low levels of protection, also limiting abatement. Larger MPAs were associated with greater decreases in fishing effort, while time since implementation had no significant effect. Complementing targets of protection coverage and protection levels with conservation additionality targets, such as pressure abatement, could shift incentives from quantity to effectiveness of interventions and ensure positive biodiversity conservation outcomes.

articles.title: Radical-induced autoxidation dominates squalene oxidative aging under environmental conditions
articles.titleEn: Radical-induced autoxidation dominates squalene oxidative aging under environmental conditions
articles.abstract: Ozone has been viewed as the principal oxidant of skin oils and other unsaturated surface films, but their fate under realistic indoor conditions remains poorly constrained. Here, we use squalene (SQ), a major component of skin lipids, to investigate the dominant oxidation pathways in occupied indoor environments and laboratory flow reactors. With exposure to indoor air, SQ decay and reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation accelerated over time, consistent with autoxidation. Laboratory experiments with ozone alone drove first-order SQ loss and humidity-dependent emissions of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). In contrast, exposure to both ozone and • OH produced nonexponential SQ decays, higher ROS yields, a much stronger in-film • OH source, and condensed-phase products enriched in highly oxidized organic hydroperoxides that closely match those observed indoors. Unexpectedly, gas-phase • OH strongly suppressed VOC emissions. These results demonstrate that gas-phase radical-induced autoxidation governs SQ aging, challenging the prevailing ozone-centric view of indoor skin oil oxidation.

articles.title: Seabirds and native vegetation drive ecosystem processes that support atoll island resilience
articles.titleEn: Seabirds and native vegetation drive ecosystem processes that support atoll island resilience
articles.abstract: Ecosystem restoration is expected to enhance ecosystem resilience to climate change, but few empirical and mechanistic demonstrations of such assertions exist. Here, we explore this topic for tropical atoll systems, combining science on nutrient subsidies and geo-ecological functions through a unifying ecological energetics lens. We show that native forest cover and seabird nutrient inputs increase primary productivity and secondary metabolism on islands and adjacent coral reefs, scaling with key ecosystem processes. We then demonstrate that seabird and native forest restoration could contribute to reducing island climate change vulnerability by (i) increasing reef accretion rates such that they keep pace with sea-level rise under a 2.0°C warming scenario, (ii) enhancing the production rate of sediment, which could contribute to island maintenance, and (iii) increasing vegetation fine root length, aiding island sediment stabilization. Collectively, our findings provide an integrated energetics and geo-ecological perspective that suggests rewilding of atolls can contribute to climate resilience.

articles.title: Sustainable solar water purification: Exploring the structural advantages of higher plants
articles.titleEn: Sustainable solar water purification: Exploring the structural advantages of higher plants
articles.abstract: Solar vapor generation is a promising technique for water purification, although the development of efficient and sustainable systems for practical use remains challenging. Here, we introduce a higher plant–derived evaporator, leveraging the structural advantages of plants and the synergistic integration of multiple components, including carbon black–coated ultrathin wood slices with perforated pores, nanocellulose aerogel, and vertically aligned wheat straws. This configuration facilitates low-tortuosity water transport within the internal framework while promoting interfacial evaporation at its surface. Under 1 sun, the evaporator achieved an evaporation rate of up to 3.2 kilograms per square meter (kg m −2 ) per hour. The material’s scalability and the capability to continuously collect clean water in outdoor environments were successfully demonstrated. Outdoors, under a solar intensity of 0.5 to 0.9 sun, the assembled device achieved a daily fresh water yield of up to 10.9 kg m −2 from seawater. With highly accessible renewable raw materials, low production cost, and exceptional water purification efficiency, this cost-effective solar evaporator is edge closer to viable, real-world applications.

articles.title: A transcriptional cofactor GRIP1 drives PPARγ DNA binding and p300-dependent enhancer activity during homeostatic macrophage polarization
articles.titleEn: A transcriptional cofactor GRIP1 drives PPARγ DNA binding and p300-dependent enhancer activity during homeostatic macrophage polarization
articles.abstract: Homeostatic macrophages maintain tissue health and resolve inflammation. Upon sustained exposure to type II cytokine IL4, transcription factors STAT6, KLF4, EGR2 and a ligand-regulated nuclear receptor PPARγ orchestrate the M2 IL4 ‘polarization’, marked by enhancer RNA (eRNA) production near multiple M2 genes. The mechanisms of enhancer activation by unliganded PPARγ are poorly understood. We interrogated cofactor requirements for PPARγ-driven gene expression in M2 IL4 , including those lacking PPARγ or a ligand-dependent nuclear receptor coregulator NCoA2/GRIP1 vs. macrophages treated with the PPARγ agonist rosiglitazone. As expected, rosiglitazone activated conventional PPARγ targets; GRIP1 deletion blunted their induction and depleted GRIP1-interacting histone acetyltransferase p300 from PPARγ-bound sites. Surprisingly, GRIP1 colocalized with unliganded PPARγ in M0 and M2 IL4 , and GRIP1 ablation dramatically reduced genome-wide DNA binding of PPARγ itself while promoting broad deposition of CTCF insulator. Functionally, GRIP1 deletion mirrored PPARγ deficiency, establishing GRIP1 as a central regulator of unliganded PPARγ DNA binding, required for both eRNA and mRNA transcription of PPARγ targets in homeostatic macrophages.

articles.title: Substrate-bound structures of yeast ALA synthase reveal protein dynamics initiating heme biosynthesis
articles.titleEn: Substrate-bound structures of yeast ALA synthase reveal protein dynamics initiating heme biosynthesis
articles.abstract: Heme is an essential prosthetic group involved in multiple biological processes in nearly all organisms. Heme biosynthesis is initiated by the pyridoxal 5′-phosphate–dependent enzyme aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS). Mutations in ALAS cause multiple hematological diseases. Despite sharing approximately 70% sequence similarity, ALAS homologs exhibit distinct expression and regulatory mechanisms. However, the molecular basis for their functional divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we used x-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate the structure and dynamics of Saccharomyces cerevisiae ALAS (scALAS) upon substrate binding. We identified critical conformational changes that occur during catalysis, regulating enzyme activity and protein-protein interactions specific to eukaryotic heme synthesis. Using evolution-guided engineering, we generated scALAS variants with altered catalytic activity and cellular metabolic profiles. Our findings reveal molecular and structural mechanisms underlying heme synthesis regulation and establish a framework for developing targeted therapeutics to treat heme-deficiency disorders and inform a rational design of next-generation therapeutic tools.

articles.title: Fibroblast-like synoviocytes exacerbate autoimmune arthritis upon psychological stress in an IL-6–dependent manner
articles.titleEn: Fibroblast-like synoviocytes exacerbate autoimmune arthritis upon psychological stress in an IL-6–dependent manner
articles.abstract: Psychological stress affects the immune system and exacerbates autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but the mechanisms underlying tissue inflammation during remission remain unclear. Here, we show that tube restraint stress exacerbates joint inflammation in a murine arthritis model during remission. This exacerbation required interleukin-6 (IL-6) produced by brown adipose tissue (BAT) following sympathetic activation. Fibroblast-like synoviocytes expressing the IL-6 receptor subunit gp130 were critical mediators, as IL-6 stimulated these cells to produce the neutrophil chemoattractant CXCL1. Pharmacological blockade of the β3-adrenergic receptor significantly attenuated stress-induced arthritis flares. In patients with RA, carriers of the hypofunctional Trp64Arg variant of ADRB3 showed no positive correlation between psychological stress and disease activity, whereas noncarriers did. These findings identify a BAT–IL-6–fibroblast axis that reactivates inflammatory memory in arthritis and suggest that targeting stress-responsive pathways may provide a complementary therapeutic strategy alongside current RA treatments without broadly suppressing systemic immunity.

articles.title: Nanoconfinement-cooperated catalysis enables rapid tandem redox kinetics for wide-temperature lithium-sulfur batteries
articles.titleEn: Nanoconfinement-cooperated catalysis enables rapid tandem redox kinetics for wide-temperature lithium-sulfur batteries
articles.abstract: The slow kinetics of sulfur cathodes caused by the high energy barriers of Li + desolvation stem primarily from the structure of the inner Helmholtz plane (IHP). Herein, a synergistic strategy combining electrochemical tandem catalysis with spatial nanoconfinement is proposed to regulate the Li(solvent) x + dynamics. As a proof-of-concept, the porous covalent organic framework (denoted as TPBD) decorated MXene is in situ constructed, acting as a tandem kinetic promoter. The theoretical simulations and in situ Raman reveal that the porous TPBD layer confines the bulky Li(solvent) x + species and sieves the spatial structure with accelerated Li + diffusion kinetics. Meanwhile, MXene serves as a negatively charged substrate that helps disrupt anion-solvent interactions and reconstruct the solvation structure at the IHP, thereby enhancing Li + kinetics and sulfur redox reversibility. Encouragingly, the assembled cells demonstrate a superior Li + transference number (0.77), long-term cycling lifespan up to 1000 cycles, as well as excellent areal capacity (>6 mAh cm −2 ) at 0°C and superior rate capability at 50°C under a high sulfur loading of 7.51 mg cm −2 . The as-prepared pouch cell remains stable for over 100 cycles, validating this novel integration of catalysis and nanoconfinement for tandem kinetics in Li-S batteries.
